rows.stem: Refer to the Venn diagram given below. Select the option with correct examples P, Q, and R :

options.label: A
options.text: P – Castor, Q – Onion, R – Wheat

options.label: B
options.text: P – Bean, Q – Castor, R – Maize

options.label: C
options.text: P – Pea, Q – Gram, R – Barley

options.label: D
options.text: P – Coconut, Q – Rubber, R – Groundnut

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a Venn diagram of three overlapping ovals labelled, left to right, 'Dicotyledonous', 'Endospermic seed' and 'Monocotyledonous'; P sits in the part of the Dicotyledonous oval outside the overlap, Q in the overlap of Dicotyledonous and Endospermic seed, and R in the overlap of Endospermic seed and Monocotyledonous. The stem names none of the three regions, so the drawing defines what P, Q and R stand for. The options are printed as a three-column table under the headings P, Q, R, carried here as 'P – ..., Q – ..., R – ...'. Page idx 2.
rows.solution:
In the Venn diagram, P lies in the dicotyledonous region alone, so it must be a dicot whose seed is **non-endospermic** (the endosperm is used up and food is stored in the cotyledons). Q lies where dicotyledonous overlaps endospermic, so it is a **dicot with an endospermic seed**. R lies where endospermic overlaps monocotyledonous, so it is a **monocot with an endospermic seed**.
- Bean is a dicot with a non-endospermic seed, so it fits P.
- Castor is a dicot whose seed keeps its endosperm, so it fits Q.
- Maize, like most cereals, is a monocot with an endospermic seed, so it fits R.
The other sets fail somewhere: castor cannot be P because its seed is endospermic, onion is a monocot and so cannot sit in the dicot overlap, gram is non-endospermic, and coconut is a monocot. So the answer is option (B) P – Bean, Q – Castor, R – Maize.

rows.stem: The scientist who proposed that "embryos of all vertebrates including humans develop a row of vestigial gill slits behind the head but it is a functional organ only in fish and replaced by lungs in all other vertebrates" is :
rows.solution: Ernst Haeckel proposed **embryological support for evolution**. He observed features common to the embryos of all vertebrates that are absent in the adults: for example, the embryos of all vertebrates, including humans, develop a row of vestigial gill slits just behind the head, but these become functional organs only in fish and are not found in any other adult vertebrate. (This proposal was later disapproved by Karl Ernst von Baer, who noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.) So the answer is option (C) Ernst Haeckel.

rows.stem: During an allergic reaction, the binding of antigen to IgE antibodies initiates release of :
rows.solution: An allergy is the exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens (allergens) present in the environment, such as pollen, mites and dust. The antibodies produced are of the **IgE** type. When the allergen binds to IgE on mast cells, the mast cells release chemicals such as **histamine** and serotonin, which cause the symptoms of allergy: sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing. This is why anti-histamines are used to relieve allergy. So the answer is option (B) Histamine.

rows.stem: Which one of the following bacteria were used by Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer to accomplish the construction of the first rDNA ?
rows.solution: The construction of the first recombinant DNA by Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer (1972) came from linking a gene encoding antibiotic resistance with a **native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium**. They cut the plasmid DNA with a restriction enzyme, inserted the antibiotic resistance gene, and joined the pieces with DNA ligase, so the bacterium whose plasmid was used to construct the first rDNA is Salmonella typhimurium. So the answer is option (D) Salmonella typhimurium.

rows.stem: The organism that occupies more than one trophic level in a pond ecosystem is :
rows.solution: A given species may occupy more than one trophic level in the same ecosystem at the same time. In a pond, a fish may feed on zooplankton, acting as a secondary consumer, and also feed on smaller fish, acting as a tertiary consumer, so it occupies more than one trophic level. Phytoplankton are always producers and zooplankton are primary consumers, each at a single level. This is also one limitation of ecological pyramids, which assign each species to one trophic level only. So the answer is option (A) Fish.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Gene flow increases genetic variations.
Reason (R) : The random introduction of new alleles into a recipient population and their removal from donor population affects allele frequency.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: when a section of a population migrates to another place and interbreeds there (**gene flow**, or gene migration), new alleles are added to the receiving population, which increases its genetic variation. The Reason is also true and explains the Assertion: the introduction of alleles into the recipient population and their removal from the donor population change the allele (gene) frequencies of both populations, and a change in allele frequency is exactly what disturbs Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and brings about variation and evolution. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem: Given below is an illustration of the experiment performed by Louis Pasteur. Explain the experiment and its conclusion.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: an unlabelled line drawing of two round-bottomed flasks holding liquid: on the left a flask with a long curved (swan) neck heated over a burner, on the right a flask with a straight neck drawn to a point. The stem names the experiment, so the row is answerable from text, but the drawing is the illustration it refers to. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
- **Experiment:** Louis Pasteur boiled a nutrient broth containing killed yeast in flasks. In a pre-sterilised flask whose contents were kept away from air (the curved, swan-necked flask traps dust and microbes in its bend), **no life arose** from the killed yeast. In another flask that was open to air, **new living organisms arose** from the killed yeast.
- **Conclusion:** life does not arise spontaneously from non-living matter; it comes only from **pre-existing life**. The experiment dismissed the theory of **spontaneous generation** and supported **biogenesis**.

rows.stem: "Different varieties of cheese are known by their characteristic texture, flavour and taste, the specificity coming from the microbes used." Support this statement with the help of two suitable examples.
rows.solution:
- **Swiss cheese:** the large holes in Swiss cheese are due to the production of a large amount of **carbon dioxide** by the bacterium **Propionibacterium sharmanii**.
- **Roquefort cheese:** it is ripened by growing a **specific fungus** (Penicillium roqueforti) on it, which gives it a particular flavour.
Different microbes therefore give each cheese its own texture, flavour and taste.

rows.stem:
Identify A, B, C and D in the following table :
| Scientific name of source plant | Drug | Harmful effects / Body part affected |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Papaver somniferum | A | Depressant/slows down body functions |
| 2. Cannabis sativa | B | C |
| 3. Erythroxylum coca | Cocaine | D |
rows.solution:
- **A: Opioids** (heroin, commonly called smack), obtained from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum. Heroin is a depressant and slows down body functions.
- **B: Cannabinoids** (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja), obtained from the inflorescences of Cannabis sativa.
- **C:** cannabinoids are known for their effects on the **cardiovascular system** of the body.
- **D:** cocaine **interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine**. It has a potent stimulating action on the central nervous system, producing a sense of euphoria and increased energy; excessive dosage causes hallucinations.

rows.stem:
(a) Identify the picture given below and name the tool under which it was viewed.
(b) What do the dark spots represent in the picture ? Explain how and why are they formed.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a grey, grainy black-and-white micrograph crossed by several thin wavy threads that carry dark dots along their length; what the picture shows IS part (a), so it is not named here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) The picture shows the **'beads-on-string'** structure of chromatin, that is, **nucleosomes** in chromatin. It was viewed under an **electron microscope**.

(b) The dark spots are **nucleosomes**.
- How they form: positively charged basic proteins called **histones** (rich in the basic amino acids lysine and arginine) organise into a unit of eight molecules, the **histone octamer**. The negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome; a typical nucleosome holds about 200 bp of DNA helix. Repeating nucleosomes form the thread-like chromatin seen as beads on a string.
- Why they form: the DNA helix is very long (about 2.2 m in a human cell) and the nucleus is very small, so the DNA has to be packaged into this organised structure to be accommodated in the nucleus.

rows.stem:
Identify A and B in the diagram below.
Explain their role in the immune system of the body.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: an outline of a human torso and head seen from the front, filled with a branching network of vessels; label A points at small swellings on the vessels near the right shoulder and armpit, label B at a small organ in the upper chest. Which structures A and B are IS the question, so they are not named here. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
- **A: lymph nodes.** **B: thymus.**
- **Role of lymph nodes:** they are **secondary lymphoid organs**, small solid structures located at different points along the lymphatic system. They trap the micro-organisms or other antigens that happen to get into the lymph and tissue fluid. The antigens trapped in the lymph nodes interact with lymphocytes, which then proliferate and are activated, causing the immune response.
- **Role of the thymus:** it is a **primary lymphoid organ**, a lobed organ near the heart beneath the breastbone. It provides the micro-environment for the development and maturation of **T-lymphocytes**: immature lymphocytes differentiate there into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a labelled diagram of the embryonic stage that gets implanted in the human female leading to pregnancy.
(ii) Explain the changes that the different parts of the embryo undergo after implantation up till (1) Placenta formation and (2) formation of three germ layers.
(iii) Mention the role of the following :
(1) Placenta
(2) Three germ layers
rows.solution:
(i) The embryonic stage that gets implanted is the **blastocyst**. It is drawn as a hollow ball of cells with these labels:
- **trophoblast**, the outer layer of cells;
- **inner cell mass**, the group of cells attached to the trophoblast on one side;
- **blastocoel**, the fluid-filled cavity.
The trophoblast layer gets attached to the endometrium, and the blastocyst becomes embedded in the uterine wall; this is implantation, which leads to pregnancy.

(ii) Changes after implantation:
- (1) Placenta formation: after implantation, finger-like projections called **chorionic villi** appear on the trophoblast. They are surrounded by uterine tissue and maternal blood. The chorionic villi and the uterine tissue become interdigitated with each other and jointly form a structural and functional unit between the developing embryo and the maternal body, called the **placenta**.
- (2) Formation of germ layers: the **inner cell mass** differentiates into three layers, an outer **ectoderm**, a middle **mesoderm** and an inner **endoderm**.

(iii) Roles:
- (1) **Placenta:** it facilitates the supply of oxygen and nutrients to the embryo and the removal of carbon dioxide and excretory waste produced by the embryo. It also acts as an endocrine tissue and produces hormones such as hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens.
- (2) **Three germ layers:** they give rise to all the tissues and organs of the adult. The inner cell mass contains stem cells that can give rise to all tissues and organs.

rows.stem:
(i) Why do plants like Viola and Oxalis give assured seed sets even in the absence of pollinators ? When an orange seed is squeezed, many embryos of different shapes and sizes are observed. Why ?
(ii) Mention four advantages of seed formation to angiosperms.
(iii) Draw a diagram of a fertilized embryo sac of an angiosperm and label any four parts.
rows.solution:
(i) Viola (common pansy) and Oxalis produce **cleistogamous flowers**, which do not open at all. The anthers and stigma lie close to each other, so when the anthers dehisce the pollen falls on the stigma of the same flower. Such flowers are invariably autogamous and need no pollinator, so they give an assured seed set.
In orange (citrus), some of the **nucellar cells** surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos. Each seed therefore carries many embryos besides the zygotic one; this occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed is **polyembryony**, which is why squeezing an orange seed shows many embryos of different shapes and sizes.

(ii) Advantages of seed formation to angiosperms (any four):
- Pollination and fertilisation are free from water, so seed formation is more dependable.
- Seeds have better adaptive strategies for **dispersal** to new habitats, helping the species colonise other areas.
- Seeds have sufficient **food reserves** to nourish the young seedlings until they can photosynthesise on their own.
- The hard **seed coat** protects the young embryo.
- Being products of sexual reproduction, seeds generate **new genetic combinations**, leading to variation.

(iii) A fertilised embryo sac is drawn as an elongated sac with these labels (any four):
- **degenerating synergids**, at the micropylar end;
- **zygote (2n)**, formed by syngamy;
- **primary endosperm cell (PEC)**, the large central cell;
- **primary endosperm nucleus (PEN, 3n)**, formed by triple fusion;
- **degenerating antipodal cells**, at the chalazal end.
